item.title: authn-bridge
item.description:
People log in at their own university, through RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche or eduGAIN, and applications get an OpenID Connect token. The same login can also have an SSH key certified, an X.509 client certificate issued for NFS over TLS, an application password set for SMB and S3, or a WireGuard key registered. The provider can revoke what it issued, and it publishes signed lists of what it has revoked; an access token already handed out stays valid until it expires. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.20.1.

go install github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge@v0.20.1

authn-bridge keygen --key /var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc.key --salt /var/lib/authn-bridge/salt
authn-bridge metadata --config /etc/authn-bridge > sp.xml # register this with the federation
authn-bridge check --config /etc/authn-bridge
authn-bridge --config /etc/authn-bridge # serve

Before v0.20.0 the command was bridge. That is also iproute2’s /sbin/bridge, installed on practically every Linux system, and whichever came first on PATH won. The module path is still github.com/go-authn/bridge.

Why a bridge

A research federation speaks SAML. Its members are hundreds of identity providers, one per institution, listed in a signed metadata document the federation publishes. Applications written today want OpenID Connect, and trust one provider. authn-bridge is that one provider: a SAML service provider on one side, registered once with the federation, and an OpenID provider on the other.

A gateway decides who everybody is for every application behind it, so most of this program is refusals. It refuses metadata the federation did not sign, an assertion that names somebody from another institution’s domain, groups an IdP has no authority over, and a configuration that would let any of these through. A configuration that cannot be served safely does not start.

What it prints at startup 

$ authn-bridge --config etc/bridge-admin.hcl
authn-bridge v0.20.1: http://127.0.0.1:28473 on 127.0.0.1:28473
metrics on 127.0.0.1:28475
admin API on unix:///tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/run/admin.sock

This is a test provider on loopback (an http:// issuer is accepted only on a loopback host). It fetches the federation’s metadata before it listens. A provider that cannot name a single institution is one nobody can log in through, so without the metadata it exits rather than starts.

Where to go next

Installing it the user, the directories, the systemd unit, the keys
The configuration every block, check, and what is refused at startup
The federation side metadata, its signer’s fingerprint, scopes, and what an IdP may assert
Tokens ID tokens, access tokens, the device grant, application passwords, WireGuard keys
Certificates SSH certificates, the EuroHPC profile, X.509 client certificates for NFS
Revocation the signed KRL and CRL, and the Shared Signals transmitter
The admin API disabling a person or an institution, health and metrics

The lists it signs are read by authn-revokd for a plain sshd or a TLS server, and by go-fileshare, which checks them itself.

What it is not

  • One process. With a state block, refresh tokens and the access tokens honoured at /userinfo survive a restart. Logins in progress, codes and device grants do not. The state is written through and read at start, so two instances on one database would each miss what the other wrote.
  • No dynamic client registration, and no front- or back-channel logout.
  • No users or groups to add. People exist because their institution vouches for them, and their groups are what it asserts.

Licence

BSD-3-Clause.

item.title: Tokens, passwords and keys
item.description:
Every credential here starts with the same login at the person’s institution. What differs is who the credential is for, and how it is taken back. The certificates are on their own page.

What the provider publishes 

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .
{
"authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/authorize",
"authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true,
"claims_parameter_supported": false,
"claims_supported": [
"sub",
"iss",
"aud",
"exp",
"iat",
"auth_time",
"nonce",
"acr",
"name",
"given_name",
"family_name",
"preferred_username",
"email",
"groups",
"eduperson_principal_name",
"eduperson_scoped_affiliation",
"eduperson_entitlement",
"entitlements",
"eduperson_assurance",
"eduperson_orcid",
"schac_home_organization",
"voperson_id"
],
"code_challenge_methods_supported": [
"S256"
],
"device_authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/device_authorization",
"grant_types_supported": [
"authorization_code",
"refresh_token",
"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"
],
"id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": [
"RS256"
],
"issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473",
"jwks_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/jwks",
"request_parameter_supported": false,
"request_uri_parameter_supported": false,
"response_modes_supported": [
"query"
],
"response_types_supported": [
"code"
],
"scopes_supported": [
"openid",
"profile",
"email",
"eduperson",
"groups"
],
"subject_types_supported": [
"public",
"pairwise"
],
"token_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/token",
"token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": [
"client_secret_basic",
"client_secret_post",
"none"
],
"userinfo_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/userinfo"
}

The authorization code flow, with PKCE S256 required for every client. A request with no code_challenge_method is refused rather than read as S256, since RFC 7636 makes plain the default. A confidential client configured pkce = "or_nonce" may send an OpenID nonce instead.

The ID token

For the client, and about the login, not the person: RS256, aud the client ID, sub, auth_time, at_hash, the nonce when the request had one, and acr when the IdP said which authentication context it used. Lifetime id_token_lifetime, five minutes by default.

Nothing about the person is in it. The claims the scopes release are at /userinfo, as OIDC Core 5.4 says when an access token is issued, and one always is. A client whose ID token is itself the credential, such as opkssh, sets id_token_claims = true to have them copied in. An ID token is only issued for a request with the openid scope.

scope releases
profile name, given_name, family_name, preferred_username
email email (never email_verified)
eduperson eduperson_principal_name, eduperson_scoped_affiliation, eduperson_entitlement and entitlements, eduperson_assurance, eduperson_orcid, schac_home_organization, voperson_id (the SAML subject-id, lower-cased)
groups groups

The access token

For the resource servers in the client’s audience, as RFC 9068 describes: signed with signing_key_file (RS256) or access_token_key_file (ES256), typ: at+jwt, valid token_lifetime (an hour by default). It carries what a resource server needs to decide without asking anybody: preferred_username, groups, idp (the entity ID of the IdP that vouched), scope, client_id, auth_time, and session_end when the IdP said when its session ends.

A token holding one of the provider’s own scopes (ssh, nfs, app_password, wireguard, wireguard_peers) is addressed to the provider alone: its aud is the issuer, and those endpoints refuse any other. A token a resource server received cannot be replayed here:

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/certificate -d x -D - -o -
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Www-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Date: Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:18:09 GMT
Content-Length: 23
the token is not valid

An access token already handed out is a signed statement a resource server checks on its own. What RevokePerson ends is everything that comes back here with it; the resource server learns from Shared Signals.

Without a browser: the device grant

A WebDAV client, a script, a terminal has no browser to send to a university. A client with device = true asks for a code (RFC 8628), and the person logs in on any other device:

client "rclone" {
 device = true
 audience = ["fileshare"]
 refresh_lifetime = "720h" # refresh tokens, off unless set
 name = "rclone (WebDAV)"
}

authn-bridge token --issuer https://login.example.org --client rclone prints an access token, logging in the first time and refreshing after that; it is golang.org/x/oauth2’s device client, not one written here.
user codes eight letters from BCDFGHJKLMNPQRSTVWXZ (no vowels, no digits), valid ten minutes; ten wrong codes per host in that time (an IPv4 address, an IPv6 /64), and ten times as many for the /24 or /48 around it
polling every five seconds; polling faster earns slow_down
waiting devices at most 20,000; past that the oldest is pushed out rather than everybody refused
refresh tokens rotated at every use, inside a family whose end is fixed at the login by refresh_lifetime; a retired one used again revokes the family and the access tokens it bought

Application passwords

NTLMv2 and SigV4 prove a secret the server must already hold, so no token will do for SMB or S3. A client with app_passwords = true lets a token with the app_password scope set one, generated and shown once: authn-bridge app-password --issuer ... --client files (--remove deletes it).

app_passwords {
 driver = "sqlite" # sqlite, postgres or mysql
 dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/apppw.dsn"
 store = ["nt_hash"] # the default, SMB only; add "password" for S3
 lifetime = "2160h" # the default, 90 days
 # table = "app_passwords" # the default
}

The table is created if missing: login, password, nt_hash, expires, idp. Only what the protocols need is stored: the NT hash for SMB, the password itself only when store asks for it. go-fileshare reads it with a users "sql" block; name the columns in its query, never *.

Disabling a person removes their password; disabling an institution removes its people’s. A removed password stops working in go-fileshare when it next reads its directory.

WireGuard keys

WireGuard authenticates a peer by its public key and nothing else: no certificate, no expiry, no revocation. So the provider keeps the answer to whose is this key, and may it still connect? The device’s VPN client registers the public key, for a lease; the private key never leaves the device; a gateway reads the live keys as a list signed for it alone.

certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json" # keys are recorded beside the certificates

wireguard {
 lifetime = "24h" # the default: how long a key is listed; registering again renews it
 max_keys = 10 # the default: devices per person
}

client "vpn" { # what people log in with
 device = true
 wireguard_keys = true
}

client "vpn-gw" { # the gateway's own client
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/vpn-gw.secret"
 wireguard_peers = ["vpn"] # the clients whose keys it reads
 ssf_receiver = true # optional: told at once when somebody is disabled
}
POST /wireguard/key {"public_key": "...", "device": "laptop"}, with a token of the wireguard scope; answers the lease’s end
DELETE /wireguard/key {"public_key": "..."}: the owner takes a key back
GET /wireguard/peers for the gateway’s own client_credentials token, scope wireguard_peers: a signed JWT of type wireguard-peers+jwt, addressed to that gateway, valid five minutes

A key somebody else holds, a key that was taken back, and one key too many are refused with 409. A gateway client must be confidential, and must name clients that have wireguard_keys. The format of the list, and the gateway’s side, are go-authn/wireguard’s.

OpenPubkey and opkssh

opkssh turns an ID token into SSH logins with no CA at all, and the token it makes (a PK Token) outlives the ID token inside it. The provider returns the nonce verbatim in the code flow and in the device flow, signs RS256, and keeps a retired key published for as long as retired_signing_key_files names it, so that a PK Token signed before a rotation still verifies:

retired_signing_key_files = ["/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-03.key"]

Give opkssh a client of its own with id_token_claims = true: it matches people on the PK Token’s claims, and its ID token travels to every server it logs into.

item.title: A token at the bind, in a field that is not the password
item.description:
go-authn/oidc verifies a token into an identity. The obvious way to carry one to an LDAP server is the password field, and it works once and then stops: the password field is where the mfa block takes the code off the end, and a token cannot be both.

So the token goes where the protocol has a place for it. A SASL bind’s credentials are an octet string of the mechanism’s own shape, and RFC 7628’s OAUTHBEARER shape is a GS2 header followed by key/value pairs, one of which is auth=Bearer <token>:

n,,^Aauth=Bearer eyJ…^A^A

The password field is left alone. On one listener, at the same time, a person can type a password with a code on the end and another can send a token.

oidc {
 issuer = "https://login.example.org/realms/staff" # the "iss" a token must carry, and where discovery starts
 audience = "ldap" # this server's client id at the provider

 # username_claim = "preferred_username" which claim names the person here
 # jwks_url = "…" skips discovery, for a provider that does not publish it
 # allow_plaintext = true only when TLS is terminated in front of this process
}

issuer and audience are required. Without username_claim, the name is preferred_username, then email when email_verified is true, then sub. With the block, the root DSE advertises the mechanism:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' supportedSASLMechanisms
dn:
supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER

Without it, every SASL bind is answered authMethodNotSupported — not this way, which sends a client somewhere different from wrong password.

Discovery happens at startup

The provider’s discovery document and keys are read when the server starts, and by check. A provider that cannot be reached stops the server where somebody is watching, rather than refusing every bind later:

$ authnd check cases/oidc.hcl
authnd: oidc "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff": oidc: reading https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration: Get "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused

An issuer that is not https is refused, except on loopback:

$ authnd check cases/oidc-http.hcl
authnd: oidc "http://login.example.org/realms/staff": oidc: http://login.example.org/realms/staff is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way

How many factors is a token?

Whatever the issuer says it checked, and nothing more. A token carries RFC 8176’s amr, the methods the provider used. That is the only evidence there is, so it is what the mfa policy counts, by kind:

amr method kind
pwd, pin, kba, mca knowledge
otp, hwk, swk, sms, tel, sc, pop, user, wia, mfa possession
fpt, face, iris, retina, vbm, geo inherence
anything else unknown, which never satisfies distinct_kinds
no amr at all one factor, possession — the token itself

Two methods of one kind are one factor. The alternative would be this server inventing a second factor nobody performed; and a server that believes the issuer about who this is has no separate ground for disbelieving it about how it checked.

With an mfa block, check says it:

$ authnd check sasl
ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS
alice the configuration file a password uid and cn
tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret uid and cn
a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds
or a token from http://127.0.0.1:18481, over SASL OAUTHBEARER over TLS
a token counts for the factors its amr claim names, so one with no amr is refused by this policy
alice has no second factor here, so a password cannot satisfy this policy; a token whose amr names two kinds still can
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

alice has no totp_secret, so a password with a code can never be enough for them; a token whose amr names two kinds can, as the first bind below shows.

What the binds look like

The issuer here is a small test provider on loopback, and oidctool a test client written for these pages: it signs a token for the name given, with the amr given, sends it in an OAUTHBEARER bind (with an authzid when a fifth argument names one), and prints the bind’s result code and the server’s SASL credentials. Against the configuration above, over ldaps://:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 0, serverSaslCreds
$ ./oidctool alice '' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","kba"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls tess
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"insufficient_scope","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}
$ ./oidctool zed '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"invalid_token","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}

0 is success, 49 invalidCredentials, 14 saslBindInProgress. A ["pwd","kba"] token names two methods of one kind, so it counts once. And to the same configuration without cert_file and key_file, on a plaintext listener:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3893 clear
bind result 13

13 is confidentialityRequired: a token is not taken over a connection that is not encrypted.

What the server wrote for the four binds over ldaps:// that were refused:

alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: the token is for "alice" and asks to act as "tess"; this server does not delegate
zed was refused: the token verified, and no source here publishes anybody by that name

and for the plaintext one:

a token was refused: OAUTHBEARER was offered over a connection that is not encrypted, and allow_plaintext is not set

A successful OAUTHBEARER bind leaves the connection bound as uid=<name>,ou=people,<base_dn>, spelled as every other entry is.

What it refuses

  • A token in the clear. A bearer token needs no other half: whoever reads it off the wire is that person until it expires. allow_plaintext = true exists for a deployment that terminates TLS in front of this process, and check then says a token may cross this socket in the clear.
  • A request to be somebody else. The GS2 header may name an authzid. A token for alice carrying a request to act as tess is refused, not quietly treated as either.
  • A token for somebody no source here publishes. The client is told only invalid_token; which names exist is not something to hand out one guess at a time. The reason is in the server’s output.
  • Channel binding. A GS2 header with p= — the client insists on channel binding — is refused: this server does not do it, and accepting the header while binding nothing would let the client believe the channel was checked.
  • A mechanism this server does not speak, with authMethodNotSupported.

A refusal of the token itself is RFC 7628 §3.2.3’s: a JSON error carrying openid-configuration, returned as saslBindInProgress so the client can send the ^A that ends the exchange. A token that verifies but does not satisfy the mfa policy is answered plainly invalidCredentials, as the second and third binds above show.

A token does not set a password

A person who has only ever signed in with a token cannot use that session to give themselves a first password, and a person who has one must still send it to change it. See changing a password.

item.title: oidc — verifying a bearer token
item.description:
Who does this bearer token say is asking, and should it be believed? Discovery, the key set, and the checks a resource server must make — in pure Go, with no dependencies outside the standard library.

go get github.com/go-authn/oidc@v0.4.0

There is no login flow here: no redirect, no code exchange, no client secret, no cookies. This is the resource-server half — something arrives with a token, and this says who that is.

Example 

package main

import (
 "context"
 "fmt"
 "log"
 "net/http"
 "strings"

 "github.com/go-authn/oidc"
)

func main() {
 // Discovery happens here, at startup: an issuer that does not answer is
 // a server that cannot authenticate anybody.
 v, err := oidc.New(context.Background(), oidc.Config{
 Issuer: "https://login.example.org",
 Audience: "fileshare",
 Type: "at+jwt", // a resource server takes access tokens, not ID tokens
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }

 http.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
 raw, ok := strings.CutPrefix(r.Header.Get("Authorization"), "Bearer ")
 if !ok {
 http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
 return
 }
 tok, err := v.Verify(r.Context(), raw)
 if err != nil {
 log.Print(err) // which check refused it: for this log only
 http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
 return
 }
 fmt.Fprintln(w, tok.Subject(), tok.Username(), tok.Groups())
 })
 log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

A Verifier is safe for concurrent use and holds the key set: build one at startup and keep it. Verify’s error says which check refused the token, for the server’s log; the client gets one refusal whatever the check.

Three configurations New refuses before anything is fetched:

package main

import (
 "context"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/oidc"
)

func main() {
 ctx := context.Background()
 for _, cfg := range []oidc.Config{
 {Issuer: "http://login.example.org", Audience: "fileshare"},
 {Issuer: "https://login.example.org"},
 {Audience: "fileshare"},
 } {
 _, err := oidc.New(ctx, cfg)
 fmt.Println(err)
 }
}
oidc: http://login.example.org is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way
oidc: no audience: a token minted for another service is a valid token, and a verifier that does not check accepts every one the issuer ever signed
oidc: no issuer: a verifier without one accepts tokens from anybody

The rest of Config is optional: JWKSURL skips discovery; UsernameClaim and GroupsClaim (default groups) name the claims; ClockSkew and MinRefresh default to one minute; Client is the HTTP client, for a proxy, a private CA or a timeout. A Token reads Subject, Issuer, Audience, Email, EmailVerified, Username, Groups, Expiry, NotBefore and IssuedAt; Claim(name, &v) decodes any other claim, and Has(name) says whether it is there.

What it accepts

Ten signature algorithms, as an allowlist: RS256 RS384 RS512, PS256 PS384 PS512, ES256 ES384 ES512, and EdDSA (Ed25519). A token whose alg is not one of these is refused before any key is fetched. alg: none and the HMAC family are refused by not being on the list, and the key must be of the algorithm’s kind: a token claiming RS256 is checked with an RSA key or refused.

What it refuses, and why

why
alg: none a token that says it is unsigned is a JSON object somebody typed
HMAC against a public key HS256 takes a shared secret, and the issuer’s key is public: anybody could mint a token
an issuer that merely starts with the right one iss is compared whole: https://login.example.org.evil.test starts with the right string
a missing or wrong audience a token minted for another service is valid; it is not addressed to this one
a token with no expiry it is a password somebody can copy once
an issuer, a key set, or a redirect over cleartext HTTP, except to loopback the key set decides every signature
an RSA key under 2048 bits, or with n or e not in shortest form; an EC point not on its curve signatures under a short key can be forged; before v0.2.2, a 1024-bit modulus padded with zero bytes passed as 2048 bits
a key published with use other than sig a key set legitimately holds encryption keys too
with Type set, a token of another typ; with it unset, a typ other than JWT or at+jwt (a token with no typ header passes) RFC 9068 §4: a resource server checks typ: at+jwt, or it takes an ID token for an access token whenever the audiences agree
a part that is not canonical base64url a token verifies as one string

ECDSA’s s and n − s both verify, as the algorithm allows. So a denylist or a replay cache keys on jti or sub, never on the token as sent.

Keys rotate, and an unknown key is not a way to hammer the issuer. A signature nothing held can verify is worth one refetch of the key set per MinRefresh, whether the kid is new or the same kid carries a new key. Tokens that need the key set while a fetch is under way wait for it, and a fetch that fails still counts.

Which name Username() gives. By default preferred_username, then email only when email_verified is true, then sub. An unverified email is a string the person typed (OIDC Core §5.1). A configured UsernameClaim is read as named, with no fallback.

What it is checked against

pyjwt signs every token in the test suite, so the verifier is never judged by a signer from the same hands. The HMAC-confusion token is forged by hand, because pyjwt refuses to produce it. testdata/fixed.json — tokens pyjwt signed once with a fixed key — lets the architecture lanes, s390x included, verify real signatures with the clock fixed. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install pyjwt and set OIDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE, so a missing pyjwt fails rather than skips. Accepting HMAC, comparing the issuer by prefix and skipping the audience check were each tried on purpose, and each turns a test red. The coverage lane’s floor is 90%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/oidc@v0.4.0
